utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I'm now going to summarise the procedure first, and several questions will arise in this important hearing. I wish to remind you that we as the Appeals Chamber have been seized of a request filed on the 26th of June, 2002 by counsel for Mr. Randal, who worked for several years for the Washington Post as a journalist. Following a scheduling order issued on the 4th of September, 2002, the Appeals Chamber is sitting today to hear the arguments of the parties. Let me remind you of the context. It originates from a decision rendered on the 29th of January, 2002, by Trial Chamber II, chaired by Judge Agius and consisting of Judge Janu and Judge Taya. In that decision, the Trial Chamber, acting on a request from the Prosecution and pursuant to Rule 54 of the rules, a confidential subpoena to give evidence seeking to compel Mr. Randal to testify in the proceedings. Mr. Randal opposed this subpoena by written motion filed on the 8th of May, 2002. On the 10th of May, 2002, the Trial Chamber heard oral arguments from both Mr. Randal and the prosecution regarding the motion to set aside the said subpoena. On the 7th of June, 2002, in its decision on the motion to set aside the confidential subpoena to give evidence, the Trial Chamber upheld this subpoena against Mr. Randal. On the 19th of June, 2002, pursuant to Rule 73 of the rules, the Trial Chamber granted certification to file an interlocutory appeal, which was filed on the 26th of June. Filings in the appeal. Following the decision of the 5th of August, the Appeals Chamber authorised the certain number of media companies and associations of journalists to intervene as amici curiae. On the 16th of August, the counsel for the amici curiae filed a brief in support of the appeal of Mr. Randal. The Prosecution filed a response on the 15th of July to the appellant, and on the 27th of August to the amici curiae. The counsel for the accused of Mr. Brdjanin and Mr. Talic, the two accused in this case, did not file any briefs in this appeal. However, the counsel for Mr. Brdjanin had chosen to exercise his right to make oral submissions at the present hearing at first, but he subsequently withdrew. The counsel for Mr. Talic did not wish to avail itself of this option. Given the importance of this case, and as a matter of fairness to the parties and the amici curiae, the Appeals Chamber felt it would be necessary to have an oral argument. The Judges have had the benefit of reading numerous detailed briefs filed by the parties. From these, it would appear -- it would appear, that the core issues raised in this appeal are the following. First of all, war correspondents, do they enjoy any kind of immunity which would protect them against the obligation to testify in certain cases before this Tribunal? And in particular, the work of war correspondents, is there a public interest in that work that the Tribunal should protect? Is such a public interest protected under customary international law or general principles of law? Would compelling war correspondents to testify before a War Crimes Tribunal adversely affect their ability to carry out their work and thus their ability to pursue this public interest? A second series of questions: If so, that is if the journalists do have immunity, what are the criteria for the application of this privilege? In particular, if there are any criteria to -- meant to protect war correspondents, what kind of information should the proposed immunity protect? Does it also protect confidential sources? A third series of questions: If there is any form of immunity for war correspondents, does it apply to the facts of this case? In this connection, I would like to summarise very briefly what took place before the Trial Chamber. During of course -- from the surface of the file, at a hearing held on the 21st of January, 2002, the Prosecution sought to have admitted in evidence an article written by Mr. Randal, and published on the 11th of February, 1993 in the Washington Post. The Defence objected to the article's admission without first being given an opportunity to cross-examine Mr. Randal. The Prosecution then requested the Trial Chamber to issue a subpoena to Mr. Randal. Mr. Randal, I wish to remind you, had already given a written statement to the Prosecution but he did not wish to testify in the proceedings. Consequently, the Trial Chamber and that is the last question, was it in error in finding that it was necessary to subpoena Mr. Randal under Rule 54 of the Tribunal's rules? That would be briefly the summary of the background for this hearing. I am suggesting the following schedule. After the opening remarks that I have made - and I think I've respected my time limit, that is 9.15 - we intend to hear the arguments of the appellant. Then from 10.00 to 10.40 we will hear the submissions of the amici curiae. Then we will have a break. The Judges will have questions. I wish to remind you that Judges can always put questions in the course of the submissions, at least for the sake of clarification, but according to this schedule, supported by my colleagues, I think that the most important questions will be put after the break. From 11.30 to 12.10, we will hear the counsel for the Prosecution; then the response of the counsel for the amici curiae, if they consider it necessary; then the reply for the counsel for the appellant, if necessary; and then, again, some 30 minutes for the questions of the Judges, if the Judges wish to intervene. What I would like to ask you, because you're rather numerous in this very important hearing, and in view of the fact that you have submitted very lengthy written submissions, I would like to ask you not to repeat the points you have made in those submissions but to present in a clear, succinct, and synthetic manner your main arguments as is normal for good professionals that you are. So it is 9.15, and in accordance with this schedule, I will perhaps ask Mr. Robertson as counsel for the appellant to take the floor. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBERTSON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour. It is a great privilege for me to represent Jonathan Randal in this appeal against the Trial Chamber's decision to which you have referred. And I hope in the course of my address to deal with the questions that you have so accurately and presciently summarised, Mr. President, namely, the first issue be of three that you have identified, being the public interests that are at stake in the use of the Court's coercive powers over war correspondents; the second set of questions concerning the criteria and the -- by which any such evidential rules should be formulated; and the third set of questions, namely, how that criteria, once identified, should be applied to the facts of this case. And I hope in the course of my address to suggest answers to those questions that have been posited this morning by the Court. Mr. Randal, as you know, was served in Paris with a subpoena to compel his testimony as a witness for the Prosecution in respect of his work in a conflict zone - namely Banja Luka - in early 1993, February 1993, when the article was published, a time be it noted that before this Tribunal had been effectively established. The appeal raises the issues that you identified: Firstly, the issue of public interest principle, we say the issue of principle, and the formulation of the criteria for the evidential rule; and secondly and finally, applying the principle once it's identified to Mr. Randal. The issue of principle is whether, as we contend, there is a special evidential rule under which war correspondents will only be compelled against their will to testify to an international criminal court when their evidence is essential to the just determination of the case and can be obtained by no other means than the use of the court's coercive powers, or whether, as the Trial Chamber held, their attendance as witness may be compelled either by Prosecution or by the Defence if there is -- evidence is merely relevant - or "pertinent" was the word used by the Trial Chamber - to an issue in the trial. Of course the final question is whether once the rule has been formulated as being either relevancy, which is the rule that applies to any witness, or some form of essentiality, whether in this case the evidence that Jon Randal could give is sufficiently significant to justify under the test that's been identified an order to give it. You will find in paragraph 18 of our written submissions, our basic written submissions - not our response - the suggested formulation of the rule that we respectfully invite the Court to adopt whenever either the Prosecution or the defendant applies to subpoena an unwilling journalist. That party before the subpoena is issued, we say, should have the burden of proving or satisfying the Court of five matters that we set out in paragraph 18 2(A) to 2(E); namely that the journalist -- the unwilling journalist, if forced to testify, will provide admissible evidence that is, A, of crucial importance to its determination of a defendant's guilt or innocence; and B, which evidence cannot be obtained by other means or from any other witness; and C, that the giving of this evidence by the journalist will not require breach of any obligation of confidence; D, that the giving of this evidence will not put him or his family or sources in any reasonably apprehended personal danger; and E, that the decision will not serve as a precedent which would unnecessarily jeopardise the effectiveness or safety of other journalists reporting from that conflict zone in the future. That is at paragraph 18 in our submissions, the nub of the submissions. That is the way we formulate the rule, accepting as we do that is the rule could be formulated in different words, in different ways. The nub of the rule that we suggest in cases where confidentiality is not in issue - and it's not in issue directly in this case - is that the evidence be crucial or essential to either the Prosecution or the Defence and that it can be obtained in no other way and that there be no, of course, question of personal danger. Of course I emphasise two matters about our suggested evidential rule: Firstly, that we are not seeking blanket immunity, total immunity, for all war correspondents. It's only engaged when a war correspondent refuses to testify. We're not seeking, as it were, the Red Cross rule in Simic that protects testimony or class of testimony entirely. We're not seeking a blanket immunity. Some journalists, no doubt taking the view that it's obvious that their evidence is essential to a case, will volunteer to testify without any issue of a subpoena. And it's clear that several have done so in this court already. The second matter that I should stress is that we're not seeking absolute immunity. We accept that there is -- there are cases, there will be cases, where evidence from a journalist and only evidence from a journalist will be crucial to a defendant's guilt or innocence of a war crime or crime against humanity. And in such cases one can envisage a journalist who manages to get in and is only the witness perhaps to a killing of a hundred innocent -- a hundred prisoners of war, a brutal killing. In that sort of situation where the journalist is the only witness clearly the public interest and the just determination of such an appalling charge of mass murder or a crime against humanity must override or trump, to use the card metaphor, the public interest, which we contend justifies having an evidential rule in the first place. But the existence of such a rule which permits compulsion as a last resort will serve to avoid unseemly and damaging clashes between the profession of journalism and the fledgling international criminal law system, clashes that will if they continue only damage the cause of global justice to which Mr. Randal and his former employers, the Washington Post, are committed. Now, it is said against our proposed rule vociferously by the Office of the Prosecutor, and in more measured terms by the Trial Chamber, that it's a new rule. Well, of course it's a new rule, but it's none the worse for that. There were no journalists compelled at Nuremberg to testify, so the issue didn't arise. International criminal justice, at least in this ad hoc sense, only became a reality in this building a few years ago after the Tadic conviction and appeal. These courts have heard several journalists testify voluntarily. Behind the scenes as a result of this case it's clear that many more have refused invitations by the Prosecution to testify and have been allowed to go on their way. Mr. Randal is the first that the Office of the Prosecutor has decided to compel, not his colleague Mr. X, who gives much more relevant evidence of the interview because he was the only one who could speak Serbo-Croat. Mr. Randal is the first of many unwilling journalists but the first who the Office of the Prosecutor has insisted should be the subject of the Court's coercive powers. They know that he refuses to testify as a matter of professional ethics, but they've taken a course that will, if they are correct, result in a spectacle - and I use the term advisedly - a spectacle of a professional journalist in every way committed to international criminal justice, who has served the cause with great courage as a war correspondent, being liable to punishment by way of contempt proceedings carrying up to seven years in prison. That is a spectacle that would confound and confuse those who support the operations of this court, but it's the Prosecutor who has decided to make Mr. Randal the test case to force this issue, so it hardly lies in the Prosecution's mouth to complain that the rule that we seek by -- to invite this Court to adopt to protect him is new. What is new is their insistence on putting him in jeopardy and in putting him in a position that invites his punishment. So the fact that the Court is considering this rule for the first time, the fact it's a new rule in international criminal law, is not in any way when considered in context an argument against it. There is nothing unprecedented or improbable about the claim that war correspondents require a special evidential rule in the international criminal justice system. Every civilised and sensible system of law recognises that the public interest may require special rules for witnesses from particular professions or occupations or witnesses who have been placed in particular situations, and every sensible and civilised domestic system of law seeks to avoid clashes between the interest of justice and the needs or ethics of those particular classes. Rules -- special rules are there for doctors, for lawyers, for nurses in some jurisdictions, for priests, certainly for children who have to testify, certainly for victims, victims of rape or sexual assaults. Most domestic systems have special rules, evidential rules for them. And often, by no means invariably, special treatment arises from the public interest in professional confidentiality. In the cases of victims and children, it arises from their special vulnerability. In the case of journalists, domestic systems must recognise - and this is a given - must recognise that their work serves the fundamental human right of freedom of expression, guaranteed in Article 19 of the Universal Declaration, and hence laws and court orders must not operate to diminish the free flow of information or to muzzle the journalists' role as watchdogs for the public. The most prominent, I suppose, or the most common consequence of that right of freedom of expression is, as the European Court of Human Rights pointed out in the case of Goodwin against the United Kingdom is that domestic laws should not formally compel journalists to breach a confidence that they have given, to expose a confidential source, because if the courts require them to do that, the flow of information to the journalists from confidential sources will dry up. But that is not, as the Trial Chamber mistakenly thought, the be all and end all. That is not the basis of the rule. The basis of the rule in Goodwin, as one can see in reading the judgement, is that it is an application of the principle of freedom of expression, which means that the journalist is the watchdog for the public, the public ears and eyes, reporting on what happens, reporting in a way which will alert the public to the danger of crimes being committed. It is not a rule relating directly to confidentiality. It is an application, the rule protecting journalist's sources, of a wider rule, a wider public interest in a free flow of information. Both the Office of the Prosecutor and the Trial Chamber seem to think that confidential sources were the only context in which journalists deserve legal protection. That is not the case. Reading Goodwin shows that it is simply an application after wider rule, and we have shown that in most jurisdictions, there are special evidential rules for journalists in relation -- making it more difficult, for example, for prosecutions to search and seize for journalistic notes and researches or to obtain outtakes and untransmitted film. In the bundle of materials that we've supplied to the Court, Your Honours will find at tab 17, the Code for U.S. Prosecutors, the Justice Department Code, which makes it erect special barriers, special hurdles, to the seizure of journalistic material. At tab 19 there is the case of Senior against Holdsworth, and at tab 20 the case of Bright, which is discussed below, which shows that courts take special care when it is sought to obtain untransmitted film or journalistic notes. No question of confidentiality but applications of the general principle of freedom of expression that the media, as watchdog for the public, should not be muzzled or that coercive powers should not be deployed against journalists unless the demands of justice can be shown by the Prosecutor seeking to -- seeking them, to be overriding. And we invite the Court to consider now how that approach should apply to the war correspondent and be tailored to the new jurisdiction, to the appearance of these international criminal courts - first this Tribunal and then the Tribunal at Arusha, Sierra Leone, and now of course the International Criminal Court, a new development in -- of international criminal justice. May I begin by -- in examining the public interest at stake, by treading on common ground? It's accepted that this court and the other courts dispensing international criminal justice would most probably not have come into being at all without the work of war correspondents, camera persons, in conflict zones and the like, bringing home to viewers and readers the reality of genocide and torture and ethnic cleansing and so winning for their victims what Theodore Roosevelt once described as the indignant pity of the civilised world? It is that indignant pity aroused by the media which has inspired the resolve to provide a measure of retributive justice for victims of despots, tyrants and those -- all those persons in authority who abuse their power in the ways that bring them within the court's jurisdiction. That profound public benefit from media operations in combat zones is ongoing. The vital public watchdog role identified in Goodwin in relation to a business journalist sitting quite safely in his office is of course much magnified when it comes to a journalist risking his life in a combat area. As we say at paragraph 17, the media must be encouraged to continue, firstly, providing important information to alert the world to the commission of war crimes in present and future wars, and secondly, to provide evidential material for prosecutorial investigation, which if followed up can lead to the arrest and trial of war criminals. And we stress investigation. The journalist's publications provide material for the prosecution to investigate and that separation of function, the journalist reporting, the prosecutor following up, maybe many years later, investigating, getting independent evidence, digging up the graves that the reporter has published suspicions about, that kind of distinction must be maintained. These outstanding benefits for international criminal justice arising from media work in combat zones must be recognised, and essential to it, we say, is that the media have the opportunity to enter those zones unfettered and that they have, when they are there, a neutrality. Now, if journalists become readily compellable by international courts as witnesses, particularly as witnesses for the prosecution, if there is no limit to the discretion of the trial chamber judges and prosecutors to subpoena journalists, if they can be dragged into courts by the coercive power of the subpoena on the basis that their evidence may be of interest to the court or may be pertinent to the case for the prosecution or the defence, then we say that those great public interests will be reduced, that it follows in practice that journalists will have less access to information, if the position is left as it is that in the unfettered discretion of the trial judge to issue subpoenas without clear rules that limit the situations to cases where the interests of justice are overriding. Now, there are five public interests that we say -- or there are five ways in which the public interest that I've identified in war reporting will be lessened if the law is left in the discretion of the Trial Chamber, if there is no evidential rule of the kind that we contend. Firstly, war correspondents will lose, or they will be perceived to lose, that professional claim to neutrality which is so important to their existing legal status under the Geneva Convention's first protocol of 1977. They will be regarded not, as the convention protocol requires, as any other citizen, the position that they will -- the legal position that they occupy under the convention unless they attach themselves to a warring party. They will be regarded more readily as spies who operate, and will continue after the conflict is over to operate, on the side that is favoured by the United Nations or by the powers that make up the majority in the Security Council - the side, in other words, that has the support of the Security Council which can refer a situation to the International Criminal Court or set up an ad hoc Tribunal to punish war crimes, which -- a court, when set up, which will subpoena them to give evidence that will help the Prosecution. It is that loss of professional neutrality which is so damaging and damaging in itself. The Geneva Convention on which we rely for the position for the independence of the journalist in conflict situations is set out in our -- it was appended to our written submission. It is I think attachment 4 in the -- in the attachments that were annexed to our written submissions, and it is Article 79, where the Geneva Convention measures -- requires, Article 79, measures of protection for journalists: 1, journalists engaged in dangerous professional missions in areas of armed conflict shall be considered as civilians within the meaning of Article 50(1); 2, they shall be protected provided they take no action adversely affecting their status as civilians and without prejudice of their right to accreditation to an armed force. In the perception of warring parties, particularly parties that are not favoured by the United Nations or by the Security Council powers, a war correspondent is a -- becomes, if he is readily subpoenable, becomes automatically in their eyes a potential hostile witness, and the neutrality and protection which is guaranteed him by the Geneva Conventions is less effective. Attachment 5 is -- shows the -- that is a general remark, and the first general remark on protocol Article 79 that you will find at the top in the first paragraph, is that special rules are required for journalists who are imperiled by their professional duties in the context of armed conflict, an indication as early as 1977 that it was thought that international law should provide a basis for special treatment for war correspondents. Attachment 6 is a Council of Europe -- it's -- attachment 6 is the Council of Europe recommendation that there should be no protection of sources of information, but in attachment 8 is the Council of Europe declaration on the protection of journalists in situations of conflict and tension. Those two attachments, attachment 6 and attachment 8, attachment 6, the Council of Europe Committee of Ministers recommending special protection for sources, and attachment 8, recommending special protection for journalists in situations of conflict and tension, establish -- and attachment 9, the recommendations of the council to the same effect, establish, really, the point that there is a quite separate position for journalists -- for the protection of journalists in war and the general rule about confidentiality of sources. That is the first public interest that is at stake, the loss of professional neutrality. The second, we say the practical consequence of routine compellability will be that the warring parties, particularly the side that's not favoured by the UN, will deny opportunities to journalists to visit, to have interviews, to inspect, to enter prisons, to do the kind of things that might lead to the uncovering of evidence, to look for war graves and so forth. There will be greater alert to the fact that the journalist is the potential hostile witness. Opportunity for observation by the war correspondent will dry up. We assert that and in our documents, you will find four witness statements by Mr. Jones, Mr. Aidan White on behalf of the International Federation of Journalists, Mr. Phillip Knightly and Mr. Roy Gutman, two of the most distinguished war reporters, who state and give examples, and they are more from the amici. The overwhelming evidence before the Trial Chamber and before this Court -- and it's evidence that is not controverted; the Prosecutor put in no evidence in the Court below, has filed no fresh evidence contesting the expert evidence, unanimously from the journalistic profession, that opportunities will be less unless there is for reporting of war crimes -- unless there is a protective rule. The third public interest arises also from the war correspondent being a hostile witness. It makes it more hazardous for the correspondent himself. We have seen how the fear of international criminal justice, of retribution, has caused in East Timor, mass graves to be dug up by the wrongdoers and moved hundreds of miles across the border of west Timor in an effort to avoid war crimes investigations. We have seen in Kosovo mass graves being dug up and bodies re-buried in a police station outside Belgrade, and in the Danube -- in freezer lorries, in the Danube. If those responsible for war crimes are prepared to destroy evidence, then of course they are prepared to destroy potential witnesses and a journalist who does become privy to evidential, potentially evidential material will find life rather more hazardous. The danger of being arrested and dealt with as a spy becomes greater. The fourth matter of public interest is that this of course is the first case in which it's sought to compel an unwilling journalist. Journalists who believe that their profession -- professional rules require them to refuse to testify will refuse to testify. There will be confrontation and clash between the professional ethics of the journalist and the orders of the court. These potential confrontations can be removed by a clear, bright line rule of the kind that we invite the Court to adopt. And we have taken it indeed from the suggestion of Judge Goldstone at paragraph 36 of our case, we set out Judge Goldstone's view that -- and he sums it up in a nutshell that like aid workers and Red Cross or Red Crescent delegates, if reporters become identified as would be witnesses their safety and future ability to be present at a field of battle will be compromised. I would support a rule of law to protect journalists from becoming unwilling witnesses in situations. That would place them in future jeopardy. They should not be compelled to testify." And so that is the position of Judge Goldstone on which we rely. The -- finally the fifth public interest is that we believe that there are dangers to this court's own reputation if it approves the routine summoning of journalists as Prosecution witnesses. You'll be only too aware many supporters of defendants indicted by this court blame the media. They certainly say that the media -- they allege the media has vilified or demonised the people they support. They claim the court is prejudiced by the media and that the case against the -- those indicted is the result of false media reports. The court, of course, gives the lie to those, criticises when it -- when Prosecutors obtain real evidence, not journalistic hearsay but real evidence from victims and the like, which cannot be alleged to be tainted by the media. But if a rule that is so flexible that it permits Prosecutors to summons journalists to fill the gaps in their evidence, if Prosecutions are seen to rely on -- to any great extent on journalists as a first resort rather than as a last resort, then those allegations will gain ground. So the court protects itself against unjustified allegations that it is affected by the media if it keeps journalists as, I say, as a testimony -- as a last resort, only when it is essential to guilt or innocence and it can't be obtained by any other means. So they are the five public interests that we say support the evidential rule, and we say that it's clear -- we rely on Article 19 of the Universal Declaration to show the jus cogens quality of the free speech principle. There is no doubt, and you'll see from the cases that we cite at tab 9 in Goodwin -- at tab 9 Inter-American Court decision that states cannot licence journalists and tab 10, the Goodwin against UK, again endorsing the special position of the journalists. And as I say, we rely on the Geneva Convention and the Committee of Ministers and other developing comments about the need in the public interest to protect journalists. So that is our position on the principle. The objections to our evidential rule by the Office of the Prosecutor: They say it's new -- well -- and unprecedented. We say that's not an objection. They say it's academic. Well, not to Mr. Randal it isn't. If he's compelled against his wishes, if he declines, he is vulnerable to being prosecuted for contempt of this court and to trial. So there's no question that it's not academic for him. They say that you can rely on the Trial Chamber to be vigilant. We say it's quite clear that the way this developed in the Trial Chamber there was no vigilance at all. It was somewhat insouciant in its issue of the subpoena without any consideration. You can see the way in which the matter is reported -- was dealt with on the 21st of January last in the transcript. The Prosecutor simply said: Well, I want to put this article in. The Defence wants to cross-examine, so I suppose we need a witness summons. And that was -- there was no notification to the defendant that they were going to summons him. The subpoena was issued almost automatically without any consideration of whether the evidence could be obtained from other means, without any consideration of whether it was essential. A reading of the insouciant way in which the court approaching this issuance of a subpoena, which resulted in a bailiff knocking on Mr. Randal's door in Paris, is -- is in the record, but what is extraordinary is the behaviour of the Defence, because it seems - and we'll hear from the Prosecution, and perhaps they will clarify it for us - but it seems that they were quite content with having Mr. Randal's article put in as evidence and they only asked the court to issue the subpoena because the Defence said we have a question about the interpretation, about the veracity of the translation, and we want to cross-examine. So it was in the interest of the Defence, really, that the subpoena was sought. Now, there was a rather -- at the Trial Chamber Mr. Ackerman on behalf of the defendant made an intervention that it didn't -- wasn't exactly clear whether his intervention really maintained the position that he was concerned to cross-examine -- about the accuracy, veracity of the article. But in the interim, after the decision, he gave an interview to an American paper the Boston Globe, in which he asserted for the first time clearly that the Defence was not -- accepted the accuracy of the report. Well, that rather astonished us because if the Defence accepts the accuracy of the report, there would seem to be little point in compelling Mr. Randal to give evidence, because the accuracy was not disputed. All he wanted to ask was some background -- he said some background questions. Well, we have for the Court an exchange with Mr. Ackerman about this matter in which we asked him in no uncertain terms to appear today and to explain what the Defence position was, because it seemed to us that the Prosecutor was insisting on Mr. Randal being present basically so the Defence could cross-examine him as to the accuracy of the translation. But in this -- in these facts that we received from him -- it's the second document. It will have to be translated for you obviously, but it was only very recently -- he makes clear in the penultimate paragraph that his -- I quote: "The insistence on Randal, as opposed to the other reporter, is precisely because Randal's report, while accurate, does not properly place the story in the context of the moment. If he comes to testify, he will probably do so." So it would seem now - and it is bizarre that Mr. Ackerman has not communicated his position to the Court, although he was allocated ten minutes to present his defence - but it would seem on the basis of this material that what he wants to do -- that while he accepts that the article is accurate, he now simply wants to ask some questions about background and context, so that the -- it cannot any longer be claimed by the Prosecution that on whatever rule is adopted, if we adopt -- if the court adopts the test that we urge upon it, namely that the journalist should only be subpoenaed if the evidence is crucial or essential to the Prosecution or Defence, the evidence obviously isn't now essential to the Prosecution because there's no objection to the accuracy of the story, and it's not essential to the Defence because they accept the accuracy of Mr. Randal's report. They simply want to ask him some questions about background. That doesn't satisfy the test of -- that we urge, the test of -- that it's crucial, and it hardly satisfied, one might think, the test even of the Trial Chamber, which was a general test of relevance of the kind that applies to all witnesses. So we will have to hear finally from the Prosecutor as to why they say it is essential to have Mr. Randal testify. In the -- I have -- as we said, I think, in our response that the -- what is bizarre about the Prosecution's claim that Mr. Randal is an important witness is that they filed 120 pages of pre-trial brief in October 2001, and in that 120 pages of the evidence against Mr. Brdjanin, there was not a single mention of Mr. Randal or his article. How comes it a few months later that Mr. Randal is essential to the Prosecution when they don't mention him at all when they set out all the evidence they have against Mr. Brdjanin? At page 22 of the Prosecutor's brief, it says at the top: "Brdjanin made many public statements that served to incite Serbs against Muslims and Croats to and terrorise non-Serbs into fleeing. Witnesses will recall hearing Brdjanin state repeatedly to the mass media that only 2.000 Muslims could remain in the city. A witness who kept a regular diary will give account of events in Banja Luka." So that it's not a case that the evidence that Mr. Randal could give, which is hearsay evidence, because he doesn't speak the language and is -- but is in any event now, it appears, not contended to be accurate, but the evidence that Mr. Randal could give is being obtained in the relevant conspiracy period, is going to be given or has been given by many other witnesses, and how comes it that this supposedly essential evidence is not even mentioned when the Court is invited to confirm the indictment and let the case go ahead? So that's a question really for Ms. Korner to answer in her address to the Court. But we say that reverting, if I may, to the questions that the President outlined at the beginning, we say that the -- there are at least five crucial public interests that justify a special evidential rule. We have sought to give a formulation of that rule in paragraph 18. We accept that there may be many better formulations. It's -- no doubt the Court will produce its own. But whatever formulation, it should require that journalists are only coerced where their evidence is absolutely essential to prove that the defendant is guilty or to raise a reasonable doubt about the defendant's guilt. And so far as the application of that rule to the facts of this case, we have the extraordinary position that the evidence that the Prosecution seeks to obtain was not once mentioned in its pre-trial brief. And where the Defence, having initially taken issue with the accuracy of the article, is now going to accept the accuracy of the article and only ask Mr. Randal some background questions. Well, Mr. Randal is not an expert witness, although he was a war correspondent in the area. His opinions on the context and background in February 1993 may be of interest, but it is wrong in principle, we would say, on any view to force Mr. Randal to give evidence if the evidence he can give is merely personal opinion, background, which may be of interest to the Court or of interest to the Defence but is in no sense crucial. The cost of not having a protective rule is a cost to war correspondents, a loss of professional neutrality, a drying up of opportunities to report on war crimes, and perhaps in extreme circumstances a danger to their own security, and all those -- for all those reasons, we would urge the Court to uphold this appeal. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABRAMS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President. Thank you very much, members of the Court for the opportunity of appearing here today. It's an honour that I will long remember. And thank you even more for the chance to speak on behalf of my clients, the amici curiae, by permitting them to be heard by you in a case which not only affects Mr. Randal and any other journalists who may be called to testify before this case in this court but the ability of all journalists to report on the tragic events that all too often occur, all too routinely occur, during wartime. I don't think we overstated the point in our brief when we said that the submission we made to you may well be by the largest and most diverse group of journalists and journalistic organisations throughout the world ever to join in a single brief. These organisations and individuals literally spanned the world. They come from five continents. They speak the two languages that are the official languages of this court, and many others. Their cultures differ markedly. But today they come as one to seek the assistance of the court, the protection of the Court. Many of the journalists for whom I speak today have themselves reported from war zones. Three of the 34 organisations that we represent are based in Belgrade; another in Croatia; another in eight nations in south-eastern Europe, including Bosnia, Croatia, Yugoslavia, and Macedonia. Still another is in Sri Lanka. All these countries, all these areas of the world have seen warfare and repeated internal acts of violence within their own countries and all of them have seen journalists die in their coverage of these events. Others of the amici come from nations as diverse as Nepal, South Africa, Greece, Australia, the United States, and Canada, and in the case of Reporters sans frontieres, the eight French-speaking places and nations in the world. In case after case, for organisation after organisation that I speak for today, they have all too often received a tragic notice of injury or worse in covering warfare. And the core of what I come to you to say today can be phrased simply: Subpoena journalists last. Establish, we ask of you, some sort of legal test which will require a demonstration by a party who seeks to subpoena a journalist before this court that his or her information is truly essential to a proceeding before you and that it cannot be obtained elsewhere. This may be viewed in strictly legal terms as a request for a privilege. It may be viewed as a plea for the articulation of a legal presumption that journalists not be called to testify. It may simply be understood as a way to assure that journalists who are assigned or otherwise choose to speak with the sort of people who may ultimately appear before courts such as this. They can take some comfort in the notion that they will not routinely be called upon to testify against their sources. To testify, that is to say, against the people they have interviewed, but will be permitted to continue to serve as journalists at their very best, independent, autonomous, objective observers who seek to convey to the world what they have seen and learned. I want to be clear that I am not suggesting any special nobility for journalists. Journalists have as many people who are lacking in competence and even goodness as the law does, but journalists perform a special function, a special service. They play a special role, and when they cover the area of war combat, that role is to describe, as best they can, as clearly as they can, as independently as they can, what has occurred. If this Court were to agree to the articulation of some such threshold test as we and Mr. Robertson have outlined for you, it will not mean that journalists will not be and not remain of assistance in the investigation of war crimes by uncovering evidence that war crimes investigators may have yet to uncover. It does not mean that journalists will fail to cooperate, as they have, with this Court by making information available to its investigators. But the prime way that journalists make information available is by writing about it, broadcasting about it, performing their function as journalists. And if this Court were to establish the principle that we urge upon you today, and it is the second point of the President's articulation of questions to us today, it does not mean that the Court would be tying its hands so that a journalist could never be subpoenaed if it were truly necessary to do so. We too seek a qualified privilege, one which avoids requiring journalists to testify simply because they might or could or possibly might have information which, on one theory or another, might have some relevance to a case. I want to be clear at the outset that we well appreciate that the Trial Chamber's ruling is by no means inherently hostile to the notion of free expression. The opinion said - it said clearly and it said without the least hesitation - that it fully acknowledged the importance that journalists should not be subpoenaed unnecessarily and that the summoning and examination of journalists before this and similar courts and tribunals be conducted and regulated in a way which will not unduly hamper or otherwise obstruct the vital role of news-gathering of journalists and/or the media. Indeed the opinion went further. It acknowledged that in cases in which confidential sources of journalists are involved, it would be, in the language of Trial Chamber, a step in the wrong direction, a step backwards, a severe blow to the freedom of expression of journalists, the freedom of the media, if this Trial Chamber were to accept a standard lower than upheld in the Goodwin case. Indeed, I think it fair to say that the ruling made plain, and if anything the arguments leading up to the ruling made plainer still, that it was the absence of any confidential source in this case that led the Court to its ruling. That, the Court said, is the heart and soul of the mentioned pretended qualified privilege. That, the Court said, related to something fundamental, quote unquote. This case, however, the Court concluded, was one in which nothing fundamental was involved, this particular aspect of this case. A journalist, in the words of the Trial Chamber, who had no problem with revealing to the entire world the accused's alleged declaration in a publication, was not, according to the Trial Chamber, entitled to any particular or special consideration at all. The Court phrased its conclusion fairly, concisely and clearly, and the conclusion was, "Once the decision to publish the accused's alleged declarations was taken and implemented by him, Randal has no right to pretend that he may not be questioned on what he published." Accordingly, the Trial Chamber concluded, this whole case has been misperceived by Randal, and I would add presumably by the later filed briefs of the amici curiae as well. With respect, we disagree with those conclusions of the Trial Chamber that I have just read to you. There is, we think, something fundamental at stake. It is nothing less than the ability of the press to cover news in war zones, to interview people who may have committed heinous acts worthy of this Court's review. If that were not so, if my clients did not believe that was so, they would not have signed on to the brief that all of them have indeed fully subscribed to. What is the problem? Why should a court treat a journalist who interviews an individual who winds up as a defendant before this Tribunal any differently than any other potential witness? Are we, as the Trial Chamber concluded, misperceiving the issue before the Court because, as that Court determined, once the decision to publish was made, Randal has no right to pretend that he cannot be questioned about it? Our position is straightforward. We believe - and we believe that the factual record before this Court can lead only to this conclusion - that journalists will simply be unable to continue to serve their readers and in that significant way to serve that court, if the rule of law to be applied is that publication of an interview who is charged before this Tribunal leads to the inevitable result that the journalist may thereafter be called to testify as a witness against the individual who he has interviewed. Here, I think the opinion of the Trial Chamber could hardly be clearer. It did not apply a balancing test, notwithstanding the language that I read to you earlier with which we fully agree. It did not apply any balancing test at all. It held that there was no interest, none at all, nothing to be balanced, against the interest of the Prosecution or the Defence in this case in having the journalist come and testify. So long as the information had been published by the newspaper involved, so long as the Washington Post had published that information, that was the end of the inquiry so far as the Trial Chamber was concerned. And so notwithstanding the conclusion of the Trial Chamber that journalists reporting on conflicting areas play a vital role in bringing to the attention of the international community the horrors and reality of the conflict, notwithstanding the conclusion of the Trial Chamber that it was the brave efforts and reporting of journalists in the former Yugoslavia that in part contributed to the establishment of this Tribunal, the ultimate conclusion of the Trial Chamber was not that it should try not to interfere with the very reporting it had so praised, but that - and I think I do no violence to the ruling by characterising it this way - precisely because the journalistic efforts are so potentially useful, journalists must understand that they should be on call to testify about their reporting. This is the way the Trial Chamber put it. These reports, the Court said, the reporting that is of journalists, these reports would lose much of their weight and relevance for this Tribunal if the ensuing pretended privilege of journalists are framed in such a way as to render the utility of their reports for the purposes of this Tribunal totally dependent upon the wish or the sole discretion of the journalists concerned, and therefore potentially useless. And here, with respect, we believe the Trial Chamber missed the point completely. The ultimate utility of reporting done by journalists lies in informing the public. Journalists do not engage in their work for the purpose of being useful to any tribunal by offering testimony against people they interview. They are useful to everybody, including this Court, by gathering truthful information and reporting it accurately to the public. What then is the problem? What is our answer to question one, as phrased to us so acutely by the President? Common sense tells us, as well as the affidavits before this Court, that sources simply will not speak to journalists if they once understand that the price of doing so is that the journalists may next appear in the dock testifying against them. I urge the Court in that respect to review the statement submitted on behalf of one of our clients, Radio B92 in Belgrade. It is an independent radio station in Belgrade that has covered war crimes issues extensively and has been at the forefront of transforming cultural influences in post-Milosevic Serbia. Mr. Veran Matic, the radio and TV editor of the station, had the following to say. It is in Exhibit D to our submission. He said, "When you make your living as a journalist in this region, with so many war criminals still at large, where the general public is still reluctant to face up to its recent past, the investigative role of journalists is particularly important. B92 is committed to reporting on war crimes and exposing the atrocities from our past. It is very difficult to persist in this important task if the general frame of mind and attitude towards recent crimes remains unchanged. This process is further hampered by reluctance on the part of the authorities to support the disclosure of facts about these crimes as well as the lack of regulations which would force the government to allow access to the needed information, make archives and secret police files accessible to public and provide legal protection for journalists." Mr. Matic concludes by saying, "I believe that journalists should be protected from testifying unless it is absolutely necessary to the case in question, as this would endanger the position of all journalists and media reporting and investigating of the crimes in the former Yugoslav republics." Another articulation of the same view was offered in an article by William Safire which we annexed as Exhibit C, in which in relevant part, Mr. Safire observed that the reason to resist becoming a participant in any proceeding such as this, the reason for a journalist to resist, is obvious. If dictators see reporters as potential witnesses in prosecutions, tyrants in trouble will be likely to kill these witnesses. As Jonathan Randal himself urged in resisting the subpoena, journalists would as a collective profession be at greater risk of harm and danger. This is not a question, Mr. Safire argued, of protecting sources. The interviewee in this case was directly quoted. The central issue goes to the heart of protecting human rights. Will courageous journalists be able to gain access to war zones as objective observers not just to tell which side is winning but to bear witness to the murder and rape of innocents? Now, it is in response to pleas such as these, pleas that are applicable in cases such as this in which journalists are asked to testify against their disclosed as well as undisclosed sources, that we come before you to ask you to do nothing more than to assure or try to assure that journalists are not subpoenaed unless it is necessary, really necessary, to do so, unless their testimony is truly needed, unless their testimony can not be obtained elsewhere. I repeat, we do not come here seeking an absolute privilege from this Court. We are not arguing that there are no circumstances in which a journalist who has interviewed an individual who later becomes a defendant in this Court may be called to testify about what was said. We simply seek the articulation of the principle and the application of that principle in this case, that journalists, particularly when they write about the sort of issues that come before this Court, and I think it fair to predict will continue to come before this Court, require a level of protection against routinely becoming witnesses to their own interviews. This is not, if the Court please, as the Trial Chamber's ruling seemed to think it was, some sort of abstract exercise, some matter of essentially abstract, academic interest. The word "academic" is generally used in a pejorative way by lawyers. This is truly a matter directly affecting the ability of journalists to do their work, the very work the Trial Chamber acknowledged had been so useful in bringing the attention of the international community to the horrors and realities of the conflict. And this cannot occur, we believe, and the journalists that I represent believe, if journalists routinely come to be viewed as potential witnesses. The affidavit that we submitted as Exhibit D by Elizabeth Neuffer a Boston Globe reporter who has been extremely active in covering and uncovering war crimes, is particularly apposite. She observes that, "If this Court, if this Tribunal, were to establish a legal precedent that journalists could be compelled to testify before a war crimes court about either confidential or non-confidential sources, I sincerely believe most of the reporting -- excuse me, I sincerely believe much of the reporting I did and continue to do on war crimes would not have been possible." As I previously said, the test established by Trial Chamber not only does not provide the protection that we seek today, but that as its core provides no protection at all, the Court did not engage in a balancing test. It could not engage in a balancing test having once concluded that so long as the material was published, there was nothing to balance. The Trial Chamber, in denying Mr. Randal's motion to set aside the subpoena and in refusing to recognise any -- any -- journalistic privilege at all, called for a delicate balancing exercise of the right to freedom of expression on one side and the rights of the accused and the Prosecution on the other. We agree. We agree with that very notion. But that does not occur, and again cannot occur, if the rule of law is to be that so long as information is published, there is no journalistic side of the equation at all, there is nothing to be delicate about at all. The standard that we propose and that Mr. Robertson set forth to you at greater length will have a number of advantages. One of them is that it will avoid unnecessary conflicts between journalists and this Tribunal or other War Crimes Tribunals. And I deliberately speak, incidentally, of other tribunals as well because I think it fair to say that whatever this Tribunal does is likely to have enormous precedential weight in other tribunals around the world as they make their determinations as to what the rule of law should be on this subject. Our position is that in a system where the Court seeks journalistic testimony as a last resort, the testimony often will not be needed at all. That is the experience of the Department of Justice in the United States. I have cited to the Court at some length the provisions of the internal rules of the Department of Justice. I want to be very clear and candid with the Court about them. They do not have the force of law in the United States. They are internal guidelines of the Department of Justice, but they have been enormously successful in cushioning any potential conflict between the press and the government by assuring that in well over a majority of the cases in which a Prosecutor might think that it might be useful to call a journalist, that the journalist was not called at all. And there was no need for lawyers like me to become involved and no basis for courts to become involved, and no reason to have conflicts. If the information was important enough, and it sometimes is, if the information is important enough and not obtainable elsewhere, those guidelines permit the Department of Justice to issue a subpoena, and they sometimes do just that, but unless the information is that important, no local Prosecutor in the country, no federal official in the country, may simply issue such a document. And it is that sort of approach which we urge upon this Court today. We think if you were to do that, journalists will be better able to perform the very tasks that the opinion of the Trial Chamber recognised that journalists have so often and so ably performed in this very area and some of those efforts, by way of illustration only are set forth in the various affidavits before you. I repeat something Mr. Robertson said: The record before you on this issue is undisputed. Journalists work frequently, aids the investigation of war crimes by uncovering evidence that war-crime investigators have yet to uncover. But primary way that that occurs is by the publication of the journalists, of what have learned. The publication, the broadcast, the announcement to the public at large is the place to which the investigators then go to get information. We have cited, and I will not take up your time by reviewing again example after example in which journalists work together with investigators in a way beyond simply reporting, and nothing in the privilege that we have set forth or that we are asking for would prevent a journalist from doing that. Now, I referred earlier to the reality that war correspondents already face grave dangers in the field and the concern by the various clients that I represent here today, but compelling their testimony could only augment their safety risks. As Ms. Neuffer stated in her affidavit to this court, covering stories about wartime situations is dangerous business. Potential war criminals might see journalists as potential enemies if they knew that journalists could be compelled at some later time to testify against them at the Tribunal. Now, we are well aware, Your Honour, that no journalist and even no collection of journalists can know for sure what would happen if certain other events had not happened. We cannot tell you with empirical certainty that if journalists are subpoenaed and subpoenaed and subpoenaed that people will stop talking to them. But we think we have some sense of the reality of the world, and what the journalistic testimony before offers to you, what it tries to offer to you, is some sense of that reality, and it is a reality that conforms, as I have said, to common sense. Why would someone such as this defendant have chosen to speak to a journalist knowing that the information would be public, knowing that the information would be published, perhaps even wanting the information to be published? Why would he speak to a journalist if he once understood that he was not just speaking to a journalist, not just speaking to the world, as it were, through the journalist, but putting himself in a position where the journalist himself would be a likely or a possibly likely witness against the individual who did the speaking? I have three questions that continue to recur to me as I think about this issue, all of which relates to the very first issue raised by the President today: Is it conceivable, I ask myself, is it conceivable that someone who could be subject to the criminal processes of this court, who gives an interview, now anticipates that the reporter to whom he speaks will one day testify against him before this Tribunal? Is it imaginable that this or any defendant would have been so open with Mr. Randal or any other journalist if he believed that Mr. Randal would later be required to testify against him? Is it not likely that combatants who see reporters as potential adversaries and adverse witnesses will start viewing them as threats, either by not speaking with them at all or by taking less specific measures to avoid any risk of adverse testimony by them? Now, Mr. Robertson and I have both cited many cases in our briefs. There is no case law in this court and to our knowledge and my knowledge, at least, any war crimes court which deals with this issue. There aren't a whole lot of cases which do. I do urge upon this court, however, that the privilege established by this court for its own employees and functionaries in the Music case is relevant in one way, and that is because the Court stated that it would "Not only be undesirable but also invidious to compel an interpreter --" and that case dealt with interpreters -- "an interpreter into the area of conflict on behalf of either party to the proceedings for the determination of an issue arising from such proceedings." The Court said, "This should not be encouraged or otherwise exist for the determination of the issue." And those words are words that we now repeat to this Court. We are seeking a rule of law that where other ways exist for the determination of the issue, where there is other evidence of the same sort or other places to go for the same evidence that the journalist should not be first approached. As regards the legal side itself, I would urge the Court to -- in terms of US precedent to focus with particular interest on the Shoen versus Shoen case of the Ninth Circuit. There are a few cases - only a few, but a few - which are now contrary to that ruling, particularly in the Sixth Circuit of the US in the case quite correctly cited by the Prosecutor. The Shoen case cited case law and basically concluded that the majority rule in the US - and it still is - is that there is a qualified privilege with respect to non-confidential as well as confidential material. Now, entirely aside from the question of the majority rule in a jurisdiction, which does not, of course, govern in this court, I was particularly struck by the quotation in that opinion of the -- and the adoption of the Court of the rules -- of the Law Review article that the Court cited which contained the following observation quoted in the opinion: "It is the compelled disclosure of non-confidential information that harms the press's ability to gather information by damaging confidential sources, trust in the press's capacity to keep secrets, and in a broader sense by converting the press in the public's mind into an investigative arm of prosecutors and the courts. It is their independent status that often enables reporters to gain access without a pledge of confidentiality to meetings or places where a policeman or a politician would not be welcome. Once perceived as an adjunct of the police or the courts, journalists might well be shunned by persons who would otherwise give them information without a pledge of confidentiality, barred from meetings they would otherwise be free to attend, and to describe or even physically harassed if seen taking notes or photographs at a public rally." With that, Your Honour, I will conclude. It seems to us that this Court has a special opportunity as well as an obligation that faces it today. The opportunity is one which as a pragmatic matter we believe would be of assistance to the Court, but I speak not for the Court but for my clients today. We come here to urge you to use the opportunity that you have to adopt a rather modest - and we believe it is - rather modest rule, a rule of law, a rule of practice, a rule of procedure, a rule to avoid unnecessary conflict, a rule which simply requires the Prosecution or if one views this in a sense -- because as Mr. Robertson has described the strange situation in this case of the Prosecution wanting a document in evidence which the defendant no longer argues is not true -- whoever wants the information, to simply require them -- in a situation in which a journalist has information, to simply require them to make a showing to the Court of the centrality of the information to the case and the unavailability of the information elsewhere. Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you well. I thank you very much. We will continue with our programme after the break. We will recommence at 11.00. We might ask some questions, but if not, we will hear the Prosecution. The hearing is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing shall recommence. Please sit down. Let me see, with my colleagues, to see whether we have heard all the arguments from the appellant and the amici curiae, which are very strong in favour of journalists and war correspondents, and we still have to hear the arguments of the Prosecution. Have my colleagues any questions at this stage? Yes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. To focus on the questions that concern us, I have three questions to ask, and I would like, if possible, to address myself to Mr. Robertson for his answers. In accordance with general international interests and international law, as it progresses, do journalists come under the category of professional secrets? If the answer is positive, that is if they are bound by professional secret, is that an absolute obligation or is it relative or partial? If it is relative or partial, which are the limits, which are the constraints? And testimony with respect -- with regard to a person who is being detained or judged for a crime or an offence, when a person is bound by confidentiality and yet has important evidence, without the rule or law obliging him to testify? Those are my three questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Abrams or Mr. Robertson. Either? Gentlemen? Mr. Robertson, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBERTSON
utterances.text: I'm very grateful for that question on professional confidentiality. I would refer you to the European Court of Human Rights decision in the case of Goodwin against the United Kingdom. It is at tab 10 of the bundle of cases which I presented to the Court. It Blank pages inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Pages 10199 to 10204. was a case in which, as I recollect, I appeared for Mr. Goodwin in the Court. He was a young business journalist who had been threatened with contempt of court by the English courts for refusing to disclose the source of a story. It was thought by the Courts that the source might well have been the person who had stolen a document, and so there was a possibility that the source was a criminal. And the -- on the basis of the argument -- of the decision of the European Court of Human Rights, it based itself on Article 10 of the European convention, which as you know reflects Article 19 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, the freedom of expression principle, and so it held that the protection of journalistic sources was indeed a matter of international law. So that the answer to your first question, I think, is -- can be positive on the basis of the authority of the European Court of Human Rights, that journalists are indeed bound by professional confidentiality and the courts have an international law duty to uphold that confidentiality. Otherwise, sources will dry up. The second question, is it absolute or is it relative? I think the answer to that is that it is limited. What the Court must be satisfied before ordering a journalist to reveal his source is that the result will be necessary, not convenient or expedient, but that it is necessary in the interests of justice. In other words, that it is crucial to either prove guilt in criminal cases or to show that there is a reasonable doubt. I'm looking at the decision of Goodwin to get the principle, and I don't know that there is a pithy expression. Paragraph 35 is the one in which the principle of the -- paragraph 46 is the paragraph in Goodwin where it insisted that there must be a reasonable relationship of proportionality between the aim pursued by the disclosure order and the means deployed to achieve that aim, and the -- because there was not a reasonable relationship of proportionality, the restriction which the disclosure order entailed on the applicant's exercise of his freedom of expression cannot therefore be regarded as having been necessary in a democratic society for the protection of the rights of the other party. And the paragraph 39 we also rely on to show that protection of journalistic sources, the Court says in the second sentence of paragraph 39, is one of the basic conditions for press freedom as reflected in the laws of contracting states. Without such protection, sources may be deterred from assisting the press and informing the public on matters of public interest. As a result, the vital public watchdog role of the press may be undermined and the ability of the press to provide accurate and reliable information may be adversely affected. Having regard to the importance of the protection of journalistic --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBERTSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... in a democratic society and the potentially chilling effect an order of source disclosure has on the exercise of that freedom, such a measure cannot be compatible with Article 10. So, one, there is an international law right to protect confidentiality; two, it is not absolute; but, three, it will -- journalists will only be ordered to disclose their source where the information is crucial in the interests of justice. In a criminal context, to prove guilt or to negative guilt. I hope that answers your question. Of course we are not primarily concerned with confidential sources. My argument is that the protection -- the rule protecting journalistic confidence is not a rule in itself, but the paragraph that I've quoted shows that it comes from the wider rule protecting freedom of expression. Here the war -- Mr. Randal's source is not being protected because the source is known. The relevance of protection of sources is of course that once a war correspondent, any journalist, goes into the witness box and is under cross-examination, the cross-examiner may probe, may get their notebooks, the notebooks may contain names of sources. So there is an indirect threat to the war correspondent's sources by the very fact that he is put in the witness box and is at the mercy of the cross-examiner in the sense of what he may be asked and what the cross-examiner may find out and pass on to the client about the sources that the journalists had at the time. So although Mr. -- it's not directly relevant in Mr. Randal's case, it is a consideration that we submit the Court should bear in mind in framing its exclusionary rule.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And Judge Gunawardana and then Judge Meron and then Judge Shahabuddeen. Judge Gunawardana, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNAWARDANA
utterances.text: My question to Mr. Robertson: Even if the rule is granted on the terms that you have suggested, would you want this Court to decide on whether the journalist, Mr. Randal, is liable -- protected by such a rule? Because I have in mind, if you look at the problem on the basis of relevancy and admissibility, the piece of evidence that is being contested is in relation to the observation made by Mr. Randal in regard to the demeanour of the witness. Therefore -- and that demeanour is relevant to the question of intention, and intention is part of the ingredients of the offence that the accused is charged with. So in that context, will the rule - as applied by you, granted - protect Randal?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBERTSON
utterances.text: My answer to that is an emphatic yes. The rule that I contend for requires as the first step for the Court to be satisfied that the evidence is essential. What is essential about Mr. Randal's article or statement? There is no question now that it accurately represents what was said. All that Mr. Randal can add - because he can't any way speak Serbo-Croat, so he doesn't know what went on between the interpreter X, the other correspondent who could, and the defendant Brdjanin - but all he can say is the demeanour of Mr. Brdjanin during the interview, whether Mr. Brdjanin was happy or angry or whether the sweat was pouring from his brow or whether he was sad or whether he was -- seemed to be -- because facial gestures can, as I think Shakespeare once said, "There's no art to find the mind's construction in the face." And so demeanour can be -- can lie, can be misleading. However, it has a marginal relevance, not much, and our test is whether the evidence is crucial, the evidence of demeanour being, A, capable of being misinterpreted or being misleading and, B, being of only marginal or very little relevance and certainly not crucial or essential. The test would be failed by the Prosecution in putting that to Mr. -- in getting that evidence in. So that yes, we would want the Court to decide that Mr. Randal is protected under the rule, because under the rule as we contend for it, he certainly would be protected because the evidence of demeanour is of so little weight. We might also add that it could be gotten elsewhere by subpoenaing X, because X is -- who was the actual speaker, the Prosecution has actually met X and for reasons unknown has declined to call him. But leaving that aside, I think the essential reason why the demeanour evidence would fail on our test is that it's not important evidence. It might be of interest, it might even be called pertinent, but it is certainly not evidence that is important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge Meron?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. This is indeed, as both counsel have indicated, a very important appeal. I will have a question to Mr. Robertson first and then to Mr. Abrams second. First, let me say that this appeal requires us indeed to consider and to fashion the proper balance between two fundamental interests: On the one hand, the ability of members of the press to carry out their essential function, their essential role of independent and vigorous investigation and reporting, a role which is quite elemental to the functioning of open societies and as an instrument in the exposure of international crimes; and on the other hand, the ability of International Tribunals to gather the evidence necessary to reach fair and accurate judgements, an ability that rests on the obligation of individuals to tell what they know. Now I turn to Mr. Robertson. And let me also say that I do appreciate that both of you are obviously trying to help this Tribunal to fashion and to articulate that proper balance, and your help on that would be appreciated. Mr. Robertson, the test that you propose in your written submission and in your earlier statement today appears to be extremely restrictive. It establishes five requirements, all of which must be satisfied before testimony could be compelled. It is a standard which comes very close to an absolute privilege. You did mention earlier this morning the internal guidelines of the Department of Defence of the United States. Let me say that in the privilege, as you have articulated it through those five prongs, that privilege goes far beyond anything which is recognised in the United States, in either the federal or state jurisprudence, but I have just noticed, and I would like to ask you about that, that in answering the questions of my distinguished colleagues, Judge Guney and Judge Gunawardana, you appeared to have somewhat modified the five requirements in the sense that you seem to come closer to the kind of formula which was suggested earlier this morning by the learned counsel for the amici, Mr. Abrams. So where do we stand on that exactly?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBERTSON
utterances.text: Let me say first that we understand that there is no equivalent test of this strength in the United States because, notwithstanding -- rhetoric aside, there has not been a war in the United States for many years, since the 1860s, for correspondents to cover. So that the situation in the United States domestic law has never had to parallel the situations in Rwanda or indeed former Yugoslavia - thank goodness - and the rules have been developed in the context of what may -- what one may term ordinary crime, possibly occasionally individual acts of terrorism. The same applies in Britain. So that the case of the war correspondent is being decided for the first time by this Court, and as Your Honour says, we are inviting the Court to fashion a new rule for the horror of the -- for the situation of the war correspondent who daily faces bullets that he has to dodge or she has to dodge, kidnap, hostile actions, and that is a very different situation, domestically. So a stronger evidential rule is not therefore inappropriate for -- to protect a war correspondent. However, having said that, our test at paragraph 18, which I read to the Court this morning, we've always made clear, is simply one formulation, and it no doubt many better ones could be suggested. And the Court, Your Honours, will have to reach a determination, A, we say crucial importance to its determination. Mr. Abrams uses the test absolutely essential. We will be happy with either test. Ours is a little stronger. Obviously it is for the Court to decide where to draw the line, but really, crucial, if evidence is crucial, it is necessary for the Court to consider it, to do justice. And I think that is the thought behind both formulae, that the Court must consider whether not to receive the evidence could lead it to a false conclusion, and therefore, whether it would be perceived as an injustice if it did not hear the evidence, either an injustice to the Prosecution or an injustice to the Defence. It is that evidence must be of that class. I think we all agree, and B is a formula that one finds routinely in British law protecting journalists' papers from search and seizure, that the evidence can't be obtained by any other means. Obviously if there is another witness who can be summoned or if there is a film or whatever, then you don't need the journalist. So B, I would have thought is hardly restrictive or onerous, but is a matter of common sense. C is a different -- I fully accept is a different situation. That's the confidentiality situation which is -- so we can take C out because we are not concerned with professional confidences. That needs a different rule. So D, that the giving of this evidence will not put him or his family in any reasonably apprehended personal danger. There are cases one can envisage - it may be that X is such a case - where a journalist could say to the Prosecution, "If I appear in court, even with protective measures, my life is at stake or my family are still living in such and such a place where there will be reprisals or whatever."
