So that is a special situation but it's a situation that I imagine would be a factor in a prosecution decision in relation to any witness, be they a journalist, an interpreter, or just a -- or a citizen. And E, that the decision will not serve as a precedent which would unnecessarily jeopardise the effectiveness or safety of other journalists reporting from that conflict zone in the future, I suppose is -- could really be seen as a reminder of the public interests that justify the rule in the first place, and what we seek to achieve by E is simply to put the Trial Chamber which is deciding the issue in mind of the public interests which justify the rule. One wants to avoid decisions that jeopardise the safety or the effectiveness of reporters in conflict zones. That's the reason for the rule. And in this case, we saw, if you read the transcript of January the 21st, that the Judges were simply oblivious of this whole dimension. And so by writing it into the rule, we would simply hope to remind the Court, the trial Court, of the reasons for the rule, and so that is why E is there. But I do not, with respect, agree that this is coming close to absolute or that this is very restrictive, and I fully accept that there may well be other, lesser or different ways of putting it. What is needed, we submit with respect, is some evidential rule that spells out the circumstances in which the journalist will be forced to testify rather than, as the Trial Chamber did, leaving it entirely to the unfettered discretion of the court and a general sense of pertinacity or relevance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I have a question to the amici if I may. Mr. Abrams, your proposed test looks more to the importance of the testimony, to the case, and the inability of the information to be acquired by other means. Am I correct in understanding that this test, your proposed test, would allow the Court more leeway in getting evidence that is essential for its fact-finding -- performance of its fact-finding responsibilities? And the related sub-question to that: Would it make any difference to the weighing process here and the real proposed test if the testimony sought would go to the accused's ability - I'm not speaking to the Prosecution - to the accused's ability to be able to challenge evidence entered against him? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABRAMS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABRAMS
utterances.text: Sorry, I'm not used to this. I don't think, Your Honour, that the articulation by me of the test that I would urge on the Court is very substantively different from the first two elements of Mr. Robertson's test. I will say that I do find one line in particular out of the Attorney General's guidelines in the US particularly powerful, and that is that in their articulation of essentiality, they give an example, they spell out a little more than simply the use of the word "essentiality." What they mean, by saying the following: "In criminal cases, there should be reasonable grounds to believe based on information obtained from non-media sources that a crime has occurred and that the information sought is essential to a successful investigation, particularly with reference to directly establishing guilt or innocence." It is in the latter part of that that I would urge on the Court should inform its decision with particular force. Lots of evidence -- lots of potential evidence is relevant on one level of relevance or another. Lots of material could lead to more material. But not much evidence, but some very important evidence, is of the sort which refers directly to establishing guilt or innocence. Now, as regards Your Honour's second question to me about any potential difference in the application of the test to a defendant, I think that the language or some equivalent of it that I just read to the Court might be of some greater benefit to defendants in some cases because there might be a greater play in the notion of what is essential to a defence than what is essential to a Prosecution. And so if -- if there was material which might help to disprove or to suggest, at least, the unlikelihood of a defendant's culpability, that would immediately fall within the realm of something which is essential, and I suggest that there is probably more that would fall there more easily on the defendant's side than the Prosecution's side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABRAMS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge Shahabuddeen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I happily agree with Judge Meron that this is a matter of importance, and I want to join him in expressing appreciation for the assistance which you have both given to the Appeals Chamber. Mr. Abrams, let me turn to a matter which you were the last to discuss. It concerns the question of essentiality. Now, let it be supposed that you are right; then ex facie there would appear to be a contradiction or a conflict with the fact that the Trial Chamber spoke of pertinence. But would the Appeals Chamber have here a problem of construction? What did the Trial Chamber mean when it spoke of pertinence? Would it be permissible for the Appeals Chamber to construe that language in the light, I think, of a thought expressed by the Prosecution that the evidence, if true, constituted a direct admission by the accused in the -- of the criminality charged in the indictment? Objectively speaking, would that be -- would the evidence be very relevant to the charge? If objectively speaking the evidence in question would be very relevant to the charge, then should the Appeals Chamber construe the reference by the Trial Chamber to the evidence being pertinent as meaning that the evidence is pertinent in the sense that if -- if it is true, it constitutes a direct admission of the criminal conduct charged and so is not only relevant, is not only pertinent, but is very relevant and very pertinent?

utterances.speaker: MR. ABRAMS
utterances.text: I have two parts to my response to the Court's question. First --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Abrams, it's my question. The Court may not share the point of view expressed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABRAMS
utterances.text: I have two parts of my response to your question, Your Honour. First, I believe as a matter of fact that the Trial Judge did make clear what his own sense was of what was before him and what the test was he was applying. There was an exchange quoted in our brief, for example, with Mr. Ackerman, the Defence counsel, in which he said about this very issue, "Well, I'm not sure it's helpful for you to say that it's important that he come testify, because if you said the opposite --" and then the Judge said, "No, I said it would be useful. His testimony may be useful." Mr. Ackerman: "Probably would be." The Judge: "No. It's whether it's essential or not is another matter." And there are other quotations to the same effect. Now, that said, suppose we were to read, as you -- as a possibility, suppose we were to read the Judge's statements as ones which amount to on one level or another essentiality. The question then becomes: What about the application of that to this case? If this were a situation where when you read the article of Mr. Randal you come to the conclusion, as the Prosecutor argues in her brief, that -- that this is a confession. Then you might well have a situation of essentiality. I do not believe, Your Honour, that that is even a plausible reading of the article. The article itself is couched in terms of the accused - at that point, of course, not the accused - but the accused saying nothing more than he had personally argued that there should be a peaceful exodus of non-Serbs but that the Serb leadership had not agreed with that and that he was preparing laws to expel Serbs from certain government housing projects. That is not - that is not - a confession. It -- one may argue from it that it bears broadly on his state of mind. It is nothing as compared to the material Mr. Robertson has presented you with from the Prosecution's opening brief in this case, which sets forth quotations from the defendant which indeed may be essential to his potential culpability here, which did not require, which does not require, any media testimony at all. So in short, if you were to conclude that this article is a confession, a true confession, then I think you'd be a lot closer down the road to something approaching essentiality. Again, my own reading of it is that that is not even a plausible reading. And I urge the -- obviously, yourself and your colleagues to make your own decision on that. But if I'm right, if the only real potential relevance here - and I believe this is what the Court said - the only real potential relevance is that it may relate to the state of mind of the defendant months after the events in question - not that he has confessed to a crime, not that he has confessed to ethnic cleansing of any sort, but that it may relate to his state of mind - then I would urge on you that whatever the Trial Court, whatever the Trial Chamber meant, even if they meant "pertinent" to mean "essentiality," that is, does not come close to that level of centrality or essentiality that would make it appropriate to call Mr. Randal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Abrams, may I just out of abundant caution say what Judges normally say, and that is to say that the questions which I ask are not to be understood as expressions of a fixed or predetermined opinion by me. I could well vary tomorrow. Right? May I ask a question of Mr. Robertson now: Mr. Robertson, my mind has been turning to your arguments on availability; that is to say, that the Court should not subpoena a journalist unless it has first taken the trouble to discover whether the evidence in question is available from some other source. Now, would you see any distinction between the principle of availability or unavailability, I think, and the application of that principle? What I mean is would you be prepared to countenance the view that it would be competent for the Trial Chamber to look at the particular situation and to say that having regard to this particular situation, we will not press the application of the principle of unavailability?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBERTSON
utterances.text: I would concede that the principle be the second condition, if you like; namely, that the evidence should not be available from any other source must be looked at realistically and in the round. And the Court's application of that principle must be common-sensical if I can put it that way. For example, it may be, as here, that the exact same evidence can be obtained from a person -- from another person. It may be that in an eyewitness situation, that there is someone else who is an eyewitness who was not a journalist. That will allow the evidence to be called. It may be that -- the other evidence to be called. It may be, as here, that the evidence of Mr. Brdjanin saying that the non-Serbs should move out -- he says, and this is a quote from -- this is the quote that the Prosecution relies on, that they should not be killed but should be allowed to leave and good riddance. That quotation in 1993 is not identical word for word for all the quotations that they've got. They've got him on tape saying this sort of thing, that there should only be a thousand Muslims or non-Serbs left in the entire territory. They've got him saying that during the conspiracy period. That's not in the same words but it's evidence that is available from another source which goes to the same effect and which cannot be disputed. So I think there is -- and he goes on to say that the state pays too much attention to human rights. Well, that may be honesty rather than malicious intention. But there is obviously a judgement to be made by the Trial Chamber as to whether evidence to the same effect - I don't mean identical evidence and I don't mean that it must be, as in this case, the same words, but evidence to the -- of the same gist or same purport - is available from a non-journalistic source, then the journalist should not be called. That is a condition. We don't know who else was present at this interview. There may have been staffers and secretaries or even cameramen, but that is a matter for the Office of the Prosecutor. I think that your question, I hope I've answered, by saying that there should be clearly latitude and a common sense application and that the -- it may be necessary to write in to the formulation in B, when one gets to it, evidence to the same purport or of the same kind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: One last question. I think Mr. Robertson, this suggests an answer from you. It has to do with your drying-up argument. Now, I understood you to be conceding that even in cases of confidentiality, the Court could strike a balance and say that the evidence should nevertheless be produced to the Court. Well, what I'm wondering is whether the concession defeats the argument. Do we have here a problem of the particular leading to the general, or shall I say the narrow leading to the universal? If an interviewee knows that even in restricted cases, he could be summoned to testify, is that sufficient to mean that in all cases, he would be reluctant to speak to a journalist? In other words, narrow as the case might be, does it produce a general influence, the effect of which is to dissuade other interviewees from being interviewed at all by a journalist?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBERTSON
utterances.text: I think there are at two parts to Your Honour's question. To the latter, I can only say this: There is a catch-as-catch-can quality about international criminal justice. Clearly, Brdjanin would not have spoken to any journalist in 1997-98, because by that stage this Court was up and running and he would know or would think that he might well be subject to this Court's jurisdiction. But there are obviously cases where politicians, people who may subsequently be indicted, find it of immediate propaganda value to talk to journalists and may overlook the possibility that they will be indicted. But what we nonetheless say is that if the journalist comes marked, branded, by the Trial Chamber rule as a potential hostile witness, in other words if the journalist is -- can be routinely subpoenaed subsequently to give evidence and has no protective rule, then the prospects of wrongdoers, political or military figures, giving interviews are very much lower. Of course, they may find an immediate propaganda value and give the interview, but cunning and sophisticated potential war criminals are much more wary and much more likely to refuse interviews, more importantly, I think, refuse facilities, refuse journalists visas or travel documents to go to areas where they may observe war crimes. That is what we mean by drying up, the shrinking of opportunities which are in the gift of persons who may subsequently be indicted. I think the first aspect of your question was the -- whether the concession on -- that the confidentiality of source is not as a matter of international law in Goodwin's case absolute, really is a concession that undermines our argument? My first response to that is, well, our argument is that confidentiality is one application of the freedom of expression principle that can be put on one side, because this isn't a case involving confidential sources, but our substantive response is that it doesn't, because the situations in which the Court can breach confidence are essentially those where the rule applies that there is no confidence in iniquity, the old equitable principle, applies to allow confidentiality to be punctured by the Court. Let me give you two examples. Where the journalist is the -- confided in by a mass murderer, say in America, and another person is on trial, has been convicted and is about to be executed, is the journalist bound by that confidentiality? The Court would say, if it was -- if there was a new hearing before the execution, and the journalist was subpoenaed by the Defence to give evidence of -- that another person had confessed, the Court would in that situation, that would be a clear case, where there could be no confidence in iniquity where the journalist, because it could save an innocent man from going to the gas chamber or the lethal injection room or whatever is favoured by the state, that would be a clear case where the Court would order the confidentiality to be breached. Or the case happened in England recently where the journalist was made the subject of -- was sent false information by a criminal source with the object that the journalist would publish it and increase the share price of a company so the criminal source could make money out of shares, where the journalist is being used, or there is evidence that the journalist has been used, that's another situation where the Court could on the principle that there is no confidence in iniquity could force the journalist to reveal the confidential source. So I don't think that the concession that I made that there may well be cases in confidentiality where the Court is entitled to order the journalist to reveal the source, I don't think that detracts at all from the argument that in respect of war -- using coercive measures against war correspondents, the Court, before it issues the subpoena, should satisfy itself of the matters that we set out at paragraph 18.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Gentlemen, your replies have been attractive and helpful, and I thank you both.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will have some questions to put at a later stage. I would like the Prosecutor to be able to present her case for the moment because we have listened to the amici curiae for a long time. So I'm now going to turn to the Prosecutor. Mrs. Korner?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: May it please Your Honours, Your Honours, can I come back with some hesitation, in the light of the -- some of the questions that were asked and the importance that has been stressed by two of your number of this appeal to what this appeal is actually all about? And it is this: Whether or not the Trial Chamber, who are the triers of fact and hearing the evidence in this case, have erred in law or in fact in issuing the witness summons against a person who made a witness statement to the Prosecution, agreeing to testify but who has subsequently changed his mind? Your Honours, it seems to me that in the light of some of the hyperbole and misstatements of the background to this case that has been put forward by Mr. Robertson, I ought to go back to how this matter arose. It has been characterised by Mr. Robertson as insouciant. Your Honours, we would say that is very far from the truth of what happened in the Trial Chamber. Now, Your Honours, the matter arose because the Prosecution wished to put into evidence the article that appeared in the Washington Post without the necessity of calling the witness. It is right to point out that a number of other articles relating to interviews with the accused person, Radoslav Brdjanin, have been entered into evidence without objection and without any necessity for the witness being called, and it is perhaps a signal of the importance of the words attributed to Mr. Brdjanin in that article that the Defence made it clear that they wanted the witness who wrote the article to be called. One of the difficulties with the tests that have been put forward on behalf of the appellants and the amicus is that it would require and is requiring both them and the Appeals Chamber to conduct an investigation without being fully aware of the evidence that is led and the full nature of the case against Mr. Brdjanin. The matter arose in this way: That as rightly stated by Mr. Robertson, Mr. Ackerman, counsel for the accused Brdjanin, said that he wished to cross-examine the author of the article on the basis that the quotes attributed were inaccurate. At no stage - and I emphasise this, in the light of the slightly odd correspondence that's been put before Your Honours, and in the light of the fact that Mr. Ackerman declined to appear before Your Honours - whatever he may have said in correspondence with Mr. Robertson's instructing solicitors has never been said to the Court. In other words, as far as the Court is concerned, and indeed we on behalf of the Prosecution are concerned, the position has not changed; Mr. Ackerman wishes to cross-examine the author of the article on the basis of the accuracy of the quotes. If indeed his position has changed, then that makes this appeal even more unnecessary, if I can put it that way, because in that event there could be no objection to the article being entered into evidence if, as he now appears to state, those quotes are indeed not disputed. But Your Honours, those quotes are -- and the Trial Chamber in making its decision - that the words, the alleged declarations of Brdjanin are pertinent to the case of the Prosecution, as explained during oral argument. And Your Honours, in the course of oral argument, it was explained to the Trial Chamber exactly why "pertinent" was the word that they chose to use, was that it was important, relevant, and admissible evidence. Now, Your Honours, can I just before I turn to the actual facts of this case, just to remind Your Honours, deal with two other matters that were raised by Mr. Robertson. The first is this: There is an extract of the pre-trial brief has been produced for Your Honours. Mr. Robertson may be unaware that there is a page limit set on the length of a pre-trial brief. In that particular pre-trial brief, we had to cover the events in some 15 municipalities with which the Court is seized. We gave very little detail as to what witnesses would actually be saying, and indeed the names of witnesses were not given in the pre-trial brief, but this particular witness, Mr. Jonathan Randal, was - it may not be known to Mr. Robertson - actually listed as a witness in the 65 ter summaries that accompanied the pre-trial brief. But Your Honour, it would not be right to say the fact that the actual quote wasn't given in the pre-trial brief is an indication of its importance to the Prosecution. The second matter is this: Mr. Robertson asked, I suppose rhetorically, why it was that the Prosecution had not issued a witness summons for the journalist who was present and interpreting. He says the reasons are unknown. In fact, the reasons are not unknown to Mr. Robertson because provided to him was the discussion that was held in private session. With the leave of the Court, we disclosed all discussions relating to the issue of a witness summons and the events thereafter. And indeed if the arguments which are advanced on behalf of Mr. Randal have any merit in Your Honours' minds, then they would be far greater in relation to the other journalist, Mr. X, who is a journalist, still a practicing journalist, and does, we have reason to believe, as I explained to the Court, good reasons for any fears in testifying. And so contrary to the assertion that has been made that effectively the Prosecution chose in a cavalier manner to issue a witness summons against Mr. Randal, that is not in fact, we would submit, the case. And the Prosecution and the Trial Chamber are very conscious of the need for journalists to be able to carry on their jobs in investigating and attending the scenes where potential war crimes take place. But that does not mean, we would submit, that a journalist is entitled to a privilege - which I want to expand on in a little moment - that is denied to other, and the Court may feel, more deserving organisations who do show complete impartiality and carry out work at perhaps far greater risk to themselves than journalists would like to think. But Your Honours, can I turn, as I said, to really the issue that this appeal is about, which is this: It is not -- or rather, I say it's this -- can I get rid of the negative, first of all. It is not an appeal against an order made by the Trial Chamber that a person testify about or disclose to the Court matters which he received in a confidential capacity. The facts are these: First, the witness spoke through an interpreter to the accused. Second, the accused made statements which are not disputed, are directly relevant to the offences with which he is charged. The conversation or interview was not conducted on any kind of confidential basis. The witness then published an account of his conversation. He was seen by an investigator and agreed to make a statement. He agreed to testify, albeit with reluctance, but agreed that he was prepared to testify that all that was required was for him to confirm the accuracy of those quotes. And he then changed his mind -- or whether his mind was changed by him as a result of the intervention of his then-ex-employers. Your Honour, it is equally not right to state that Mr. Randal was unaware that a witness summons was going to be applied for and served upon him. Your Honour, he was told in no uncertain terms by the investigator. And that was raised at the lower court. There were two conversations with him to attempt to persuade him, to change his mind and testify voluntarily, and he was informed by that investigator that a witness summons would be applied for. Now, Your Honours, as regards the question of evidence in this case, both parties have said that the statements that they have produced in support of their brief are not contested by the Prosecution. Your Honour, that in one sense is incorrect, and I made that clear at the lower court; that we did not accept a great deal of what was said in those statements; that if any weight was to be attached to them, we would wish them to attend for cross-examination. But Your Honours, we have not done so for this reason: It is our submission that the facts of this case do not require that these witnesses attend. But I cannot let pass Mr. Randal's assertion, if it is his assertion, that he had no notice that a witness summons would be applied for. Now, Your Honours, were not Mr. Randal a journalist, on the set of facts that I've just outlined to Your Honours, it is our submission that Your Honours would have had no hesitation in upholding the Trial Chamber's decision to issue a witness summons. There would have been absolutely no reason at all. This appeal would never have been contemplated. But because he is or was at the time a journalist, the Court is now being asked to grant him a privilege against testifying. And effectively in the test which is set out in the appellant's brief at paragraph 18, the onus of satisfying those tests would rest not on the journalist - and as I understand it, this is a special rule of law which is to apply to journalists who are in what is described as war zones - but the onus would be on the person wishing to call him to show why his privilege, his limited privilege maybe, should not apply. And I emphasise the party calling him because it has already been set out or raised what is the case if it is the Defence who wish to call him, as opposed to the Prosecution. Now, Your Honours, our submission would be that such a privilege, such an application of these tests, would be to give journalists a form of privilege granted to no other class of person who happened to be in a position to witness crimes which come before an international tribunal. That would include civilians who happened to be in the area, who are just as reluctant as the journalist to testify but are granted none of these benefits that a journalist, because he is a journalist, is about to be given. Your Honours, if that test is applicable because of the public interest in knowledge of war crimes being disseminated, then why is that privilege as such not to be given to organisations such as Human Rights Watch, who equally send people into areas of danger to gather information which they then publish? What used to be called the European Community Monitoring Mission, now the European Union Monitoring Mission, who had people in the area throughout the conflict, they do not claim for their employees any kind of immunity or special tests to be adopted before the persons there may testify. There has already been an example in the Brdjanin case of one of their employees testifying to the Court about what he saw. ECMM do not take the view that that places their operations in jeopardy, their personnel in jeopardy. A very special case is of course the International Committee of the Red Cross, which has been decided before this Court in the Simic case, but there are very special reasons which are clearly set out in the judgement and which I don't need to go into again, one of which is, of course, that this is an international organisation, recognised under the Geneva Conventions. But Your Honours, as I say, the first question is: What is the rationale behind giving journalists this type of privilege which may hamper the courts in their fact-finding missions? What about other individuals, politicians who go to areas of conflict in order to find out what is happening, in order to publish what is going on? No such privilege has ever been granted or asked for by them. Now, Your Honours, if one looks, then, at the test that is set out as a suggested test for granting that privilege, Your Honours, the problems become even more acute, if I can put it that way. Your Honours, the first is this: That the first test that is set out, is the evidence which a journalist can give of crucial importance to its determination of a defendant's guilt or innocence? How is that determination to be made at the stage of the trial when a journalist is due to testify? Is the Court to examine all the evidence and weigh up the relative importance within that evidence and presumably, if called on behalf of the Prosecution, before they have heard the Defence case? Is the Court at that stage able to make the determination on the basis of evidence it's heard so far, on the basis of what's been said in the pre-trial brief, as to whether that evidence will be crucial or not in the determination of the guilt or innocence of an accused? Second test: Which evidence cannot be obtained by any other means or from any other witness? What is the Court supposed to do in order to satisfy itself of that? If the Prosecution say that evidence cannot be obtained by any other means, is the Court then supposed to go through a list of potential means, do its own investigations, or from any other witness? How is the Court to ascertain whether that is possible? And this is particularly true, as I know that Your Honours are aware, of the trials before this Court, where evidence is continuously coming to light, as it were, in a drip-freed process. From the early days of this Court through until now, the nature of the evidence that's been received by the Court has changed dramatically because of the political circumstances, for example. Your Honours, test number 3, or C: The giving of this evidence by the journalist will not require breach of any obligation of confidence. Well, as Mr. Robertson concedes, it has absolutely no application to the facts of this case, and it's apparent from all the authorities, including Goodwin - and I will return to the case of Goodwin because it's clearly a seminal case on this topic in international human rights - that all authorities have concentrated on this issue of confidentiality, and no court, with the greatest deference to the persuasive and cogent arguments of Mr. Abrams, even in the United States, no court has sought to extend this type of privilege that is asked for beyond the issue of confidentiality. The International Criminal Court statute, when dealing with - and that's enclosed in the Defence brief - the issue of confidentiality, talks about lawyers, doctors and priests -- men of religion, I think it's stated. It doesn't mention journalists. The appellant puts it on the basis, well, it doesn't exclude journalists. No, well, it doesn't exclude an awful lot of other people either, but the fact is that seeing, we would submit, the problems, they have limited that class of person or that class of information which is exempt to the well-known, recognised classes of confidential material. Test number 5: That the giving of this evidence will not put him or his family or sources in any reasonably apprehended personal danger. Well, Your Honours, of course, that is one of the tests that the Court takes into account, not just with journalists but with any witnesses. The Court is well aware, having dealt with witnesses from the former Yugoslavia, of the dangers which are inherent in many of them testifying before this Court. And Your Honours, again, how would it look to those witnesses who do testify, at great and obvious personal risks to themselves sometimes, if journalists were given this exemption from testifying because it puts them in danger, whereas they come up and give evidence without having really the possibility of such an exemption? Your Honour, E: That the decision will not serve as a precedent which would unnecessarily jeopardise the effectiveness or safety of other journalists reporting from that conflict zone in the future. Now, Your Honours, the point about the press is really this: They report within circumstances sometimes of great personal danger. There is no question about that. And we wouldn't seek for one moment to suggest otherwise. But there is no empirical evidence to suggest that the dangers arise from the knowledge that warring parties will have that a journalist may testify against them. We would submit that the dangers arise, firstly, if the warring parties don't want any publication of what is happening in the newspapers. And secondly, once that publication has been made, then those dangers are already there and ready to be seen. Your Honours, the difficulty is this - and this is particularly true of many of the cases that this Court is dealing with - that politicians and leaders want to speak to the press. They want to use the press for their own purposes, to spread, for example, propaganda, and propaganda is a very strong feature of the Prosecution's case against Mr. Brdjanin. The quotes that are attributed to him, which, for example, that no more than 2, 3 per cent of Muslims should be allowed to remain in Banja Luka, are important ones. Mr. Robertson said, "But they have that on tape." Regrettably, we don't have that on tape. We have other quotes on tape. We have other quotes by Mr. Brdjanin in various newspapers, but not that particular one, and that is why, contrary to what Mr. Robertson asserts, anything that is actually in print is of importance in this case, because otherwise, it is dependent very much on witness recollection of some events ten years ago. But Your Honours, for the appellant to suggest that it is the idea that journalists may testify which will put them in danger, we would submit, is unsupported by any evidence to that effect, and indeed, the fact that journalists have testified, apparently without any danger, we would submit, proves to the contrary. Your Honours, the fact is that those tests, we would submit, are unclear in themselves and would lead to difficulties for the Court to enforce it. One of the things about formulating a legal test to be applied is that it must be clear what its parameters are and to whom it applies. Your Honours, for these purposes, what constitutes -- if Your Honours were to formulate a test that would give journalists an unqualified immunity, journalists working in -- I'm sorry, a qualified immunity, journalists working in a war zone, what would define for these purposes a journalist? Would it be someone who was in full-time employment, paid by a newspaper or a magazine? Would it encompass a person contracted to write a series of articles for a publication? Would it cover a person who not contracted, not on the payroll of a newspaper or television station, in fact submitted a series of articles which were then published? What constitutes for these purposes a war zone? Is it a place where war has been declared? Is it a place where there is heavy fighting? If so, what is defined as "heavy fighting"? Does it cover hostage situations? Your Honours, one could go on forever asking effectively what are rhetorical questions, but we submit to Your Honours that you're being asked to formulate a legal test, a legal concept, which has enormous difficulties in its application and we would submit is in fact unnecessary and should not from the point of the public interest of other persons in the same position be granted to this particular class of person. Now, Your Honours, the applicable law as really I think is accepted by all sides is to this effect: There is no direct authority on this type of situation, either in national jurisdictions or in international jurisdictions. The question that Your Honours, or Mr. President posed, the five questions: Does a war correspondent have immunity? We would answer respectfully, no, neither under customary international law or any other system of law. Question two: Is there a public interest? Yes, there is a public interest in journalists being able to cover war areas and bring to the attention of the public the abuses of human rights, the killings, the ethnic cleansing and the like. But Your Honours, it's only one of many competing public interests. There is a public interest in not allowing criminals to make statements to the press in the confident belief that this can never become admissible evidence in a court of law. There is a public interest in seeing wrongdoers punished for their acts and in evidence that is relevant to their wrongdoing being put before the courts that have to make their decision. There is a public interest in, as it were, equitable distribution of the ability to refrain from testifying when required. And Your Honours, when one compares those competing interests, we would submit that journalists are entitled to no special privileges. Your Honour, the further questions you asked really depend on the application. If Your Honours decide that there is to be some kind of immunity, what are the criteria? Your Honours, we would find it extremely difficult to formulate what the criteria should be. For the reasons already given, we would submit that the tests set out there would require the courts to carry out an impossible, lengthy, and really time-consuming exercise. But Your Honours, what we would submit is Your Honours should look at the actual facts of this particular case and appeal. And Your Honours, even under, as we have already submitted, any tests or the tests formulated by the appellants' lawyers and supported by the amicus, under any test Mr. Randal would not fulfil those criteria. It is of, whether crucial or not - and Your Honour, we would certainly quarrel with that test - but it is relevant, important evidence which goes directly to the issue -- one of the issues the Trial Chamber has to decide, which is Mr. Brdjanin's state of mind in relation to one of the offences at the very least with which he is charged, namely deportations and forced transfer, for persecutions generally. And we would invite Your Honours to look at the words attributed to him. Your Honours, can that evidence be obtained by any other means from any other witness? Yes, in theory. It could be obtained from the other journalist who was present. But if Mr. Randal can't testify or shouldn't have to testify, even less should this gentleman. And one of the things is that this gentleman has never made a statement to the Prosecution in which he agreed to testify. C, I do not have to trouble with. D, no evidence at all that giving of evidence would put himself or his family or any sources in any danger and that the decision will not serve as a precedent. Your Honour, may I make this absolutely clear. Nobody is talking here about routinely summoning witness -- journalists to testify. There was lengthy discussion, which has not been put before Your Honours, about this matter. And at one stage indeed the Prosecution made it absolutely clear that they did not wish to put Mr. Randal into the witness box unless absolutely necessary and if the Defence insisted. Now, Your Honour, it is the right of the Defence to have Mr. Randal called if they so require it. I want to make it absolutely clear: The Prosecution are only proposing to call him in order to put into evidence the article that he wrote.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And finally, Your Honour, the decision will not -- yes, I've dealt with that one. Your Honours, those are the submissions that we would wish to put before Your Honours. Your Honours, I intended to go through Goodwin, but I think it's fairly clear. It's our submission that it doesn't support the interpretation that Mr. Robertson put upon it. Your Honours, what it clearly deals with is again confidentiality, and it doesn't seek, we would submit, to extend that principle any further. Your Honours, as regards the American cases, which with a great deal of trepidation I touch upon because it's not my area of practice. But I'm assisted by Mr. Black on this. Our submissions are clearly set out in the brief, but can I say this: It is our submission that under US law, Branzburg is the controlling case, and that supports the submissions that we make. There is a recent case which is also enclosed in the bundle of authorities of the United States against Smith, which examined, as it were, the parameters of Branzburg. Your Honours, I am, like Mr. Robertson, more familiar with United Kingdom law, and the courts there, even after Goodwin, in which Mr. Robertson acted apparently, have been careful but nonetheless have summonsed journalists to give evidence not only in criminal cases but also in civil cases. And indeed - and I think we enclosed it with our brief - there was a very, very recent case indeed where a journalist was summoned to give evidence or to hand over confidential information and when refusing to do so was threatened with contempt proceedings. So Your Honours, each national jurisdiction has slightly differing applicable rules, but of course Your Honours are not bound by that, save to this extent: We would submit that Your Honours should be cautious before extending a privilege to a class of person which is not available to others who face identical risks and which may have difficulties or which -- in formulating this privilege which may provide for the courts real difficulty in interpretation and for those who would wish to be covered by such a test. Your Honours, those are the submissions that we make.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Ms. Korner. We will now hear the responses, and I first turn to the representatives of the amici curiae. Each one will have about ten minutes. Mr. Abrams, would you like to take the floor?

utterances.speaker: MR. ABRAMS
utterances.text: Your Honours, many of the points made by Ms. Korner are ones which have led to considerable thought on the part of those jurists to whom it has fallen to implement the sort of qualified privilege that we have sought here. It is not always easy, but it is possible and it has been done, to define who is a journalist for purposes of making a determination of who receives the benefit, as it were, of such a privilege. Usually the definition has involved people who gather information for dissemination to others. Sometimes it has involved being a regularly paid employee of a newspaper or publication. I don't want to minimise the task of making some of the decisions, but they are all solvable problems and they are all dealt with routinely in any jurisdiction that has adopted a qualified privilege for either confidential sources or non-confidential sources, because the confidential-source privilege, which to be sure arises much more often than the non-confidential-source one, also has generally required an assessment by a court of who is entitled to the privilege, what is the scope of the privilege, what is the application of the privilege to a particular set of facts. And so courts routinely make determinations on essentiality, for example, and they make it early and they give prosecutors a lot of leeway too, and if a prosecutor comes in and says, "This information is essential to my case, and here is why," a court does not conduct a full-fledged factual hearing but does require at least a prima facie showing by the prosecutor that this information is of such centrality to the case as to lead to the conclusion that the test embodied in such a privilege has been met. That is, in short, a solvable problem which is routinely solved in every confidential-source case, as well as non-confidential-source case, in which any such privilege applies. Whatever the language, whether the language is necessity or essentiality or critical need or whatever, a judge is obliged to have a look and make a determination and to make it at an early stage in the proceeding. Else there is no privilege. The opposite side of what Ms. Korner says is that there cannot be a privilege at all, there cannot be any protection at all, unless a court is prepared to sit and listen to the prosecutor or defence counsel make such a proffer. Now, in this case, we have a very odd situation, and I can't help but comment on it, even from my amici curiae status. Counsel said to you at the very beginning of her presentation that if Mr. Ackerman has changed his position, then this appeal is really odd, because the only issue, she said, was truth as to the article. His only issue, not hers, was truth. Well, he has had a chance to appear here today. He has had a chance to file papers with you today. You have before you an unanswered communication from him acknowledging that the article is true. The answer to that, then, is not to say, as counsel has, that therefore the -- this appeal is odd. The answer to it is that this appeal, on that grounds alone, could be sustained. What is the problem here? She wants the evidence in -- she wants the material in evidence. The objection to it was that it might not be true. That objection no longer exists. The material should go in evidence. In any event, there is no need for the journalist, and there is no need for the journalist in particular, if the Court were to decide, as we urge it to, that when the determination is made as to when a journalist may be subpoenaed, there should be some threshold showing made by the party that needs the journalist. The Prosecution doesn't need Mr. Randal. The Prosecution simply wants this piece of paper in evidence. The Prosecution shouldn't even be the problem here, or to put it differently, there shouldn't be a problem here, but if there is, it is, I believe, resolved by the application of either the sort of test that Mr. Robertson and I in somewhat different language have set forth, or indeed perhaps even an easier test than that, but on no account, in this situation, we would urge upon you, should Mr. Randal be obliged to come and testify. A final point. The query was made: What is the rationale for this privilege? Why journalists? Why journalists especially? There are other people out there in the field. There are other people who are in harm's way. The answer is that journalists go into harm's way for the purpose of recounting to the public what they have seen, what they come to learn, what they believe it is useful for the public to know. And journalists, like the Red Cross in this one way, journalists at their best have the three attributes cited by this Court in the Simic case: Neutrality, impartiality and independence. Journalists are not human rights workers. They help with human rights sometimes, but that they do not go to an area to fulfil a human rights function. They go to an area to engage in reportage to the public, and that function, in turn, is often, as everyone has now acknowledged, of enormous help to the cause of human rights and the enforcement of international criminal law against the abuse of human rights. Journalists don't happen to be in an area in which terrible things are happening. They are not the same in that respect as the civilians who are subjected to terrible deprivations and war crimes of the sort that come before this Court. They go there for the very purpose of gathering information to report it to the public. And if we are right in saying that they would be significantly impaired if potential defendants in this Court come to view them as potential witnesses against them, then there would be a significant loss to the public, if that were to happen. It is, I would urge upon this Court, in conclusion, it is a good thing, not a bad, for journalists to interview bad people sometimes, for journalists to interview even the sort of people that wind up here as defendants, even the sort of people that wind up as convicted defendants in this Court. The public is served by having those sorts of interviews published, and that sort of information revealed, not to say all the other information published and the other information revealed that journalists in war zones gather. So we would urge on you to provide a level of legal protection, whatever the language you think is most appropriate, a level of legal protection to permit journalists to continue their pursuit of what I will call a sort of journalistic truth about the events that occur in the field and in the state of mind of people who are prepared to talk to the journalists. One thing I think is plain. They cannot have access to people if the people believe they will testify against them. That cannot be the role of journalists. And there is nothing in that respect special about the facts of this case. There is no proof of centrality at all. I've been sitting here reading the article again to myself, and I urge upon you that you should, in your due consideration of this case, provide the level of legal protection that we have sought here. For my clients, they don't come here so much in support of Mr. Randal, even though they think Mr. Randal should prevail on this, as in support of a principle. The principle is that journalists, including but by no means limited to Mr. Randal, cannot be made to appear in this Court on a showing of this sort. Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robertson? Do you wish to say anything? Mr. Robertson? Briefly, please. You're not going to replead, please. You will just respond to the few points that have been made by the Prosecution. Do you have anything to add in relation to what Ms. Korner has said?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBERTSON
utterances.text: Finally, the last point that Mr. Abrams made is an important answer. Journalists go into harm's way, often in a country other than their own, to bring out the news, and they go in to harm's way armed with the protection that international law affords them through the jus cogens quality of Article 19 of the universal declaration and its reflection in all other human rights treaties. They are in that respect different to the citizen or the civilian who is caught up in a massacre and can testify against -- about it later. The citizen's task is not to collect information. They are different, very different, to the monitor, the European monitor, and the human rights worker. Ms. Korner asked why should they not have the protection? A very good reason. They actually go there to -- so that their presence will deter war crimes by virtue of the fact that they are there to testify about them later. They make no bones about the fact that that's why they are there, because if any war crimes are committed, they are going to tell -- they are going to be there as witnesses in some court in the future. So of course they don't want or obtain the privilege. They don't, because they go there precisely for that reason. A few other matters that need correction. The Prosecutor said well, the problem is deciding centrality at an early stage. In the Kordic case this Chamber said that questions of admissibility must be decided when the material is proffered, but of course that doesn't prevent the Court revisiting it. It would have been perfectly possible for the Trial Chamber in this case to admit the article and see whether it becomes central or not subsequently and consider or revisit the question of calling Mr. Randal if the veracity of it had been impugned. But there was no -- and I described insouciant the behaviour of the Court in the -- and I don't resile from that at all. And I invite Your Honours simply to look at the transcript for Monday, the 21st of January, 2002, which shows Ms. Korner without any notice to Mr. Randal -- he had no idea that this was coming up, otherwise I would have represented him on the 21st of January. Ms. Korner says, "Well, the witness declines to attend. He's a journalist, and we apply for a witness summons." Mr. Ackerman makes noises about newspaper articles being notoriously unreliable. He wants to cross-examine, but it turns out that he hasn't read it. So the case is put over until the 25th, when he has read it. It's heard on the 25th of January, when he says, "I'm very embarrassed. I haven't read it." And then on Monday, the 28th January Mr. Ackerman says, "The position I'm taking after consultation is the journalist must be brought here because there are some matters that need to be fleshed out with him on cross-examination regarding interpretation primarily." That's -- that's it. The Judge says, "Okay, it will be signed today." End of story. That is such a rudimentary proceeding. There is no examination of why the journalist doesn't want to testify, of the issues that are involved, the public interests involved. Mr. Ackerman has never asked. Under Rule 90 cross-examination has to be relevant and has to be directed to clear matters. Mr. Ackerman has never asked what he wants to put to Mr. Randal or why it's so important. There is no inquiry whatsoever undertaken by the Trial Chamber, and so the problem -- the importance of having a rule means that there will be in future be such inquiries and matters can be clarified. We're left in this -- Your Honours are left in this bizarre position where Mr. Ackerman signs a letter saying, I accept that the quotations are accurate. Ms. Korner today says, well, we don't know about that. As far as we are concerned, these quotes are disputed. Of course if they are disputed and if the matter is going to be decided on that basis, we rely upon the case of Kordic, which is binding on this Chamber, as -- since Mr. Randal can't speak the language, he cannot verify the quotes other than by way of demeanour, as was put to me earlier, or by his knowledge of X's fluency. And we say that that would mean that his evidence cannot have the indicia of reliability that Kordic spoke about as being an indication of its significance. It was not given under oath. It was not subject to cross-examination. And it's made through a translator who has no formal qualifications as a translator. So on any view, even if we assume that the quotes are disputed, the evidence that Mr. Randal can give to stand them up is lacking in the indicia that Kordic looked for as being relevant and admissible evidence. So really again, centrality is not here. The pre-trial brief. We will put in some ten pages of the pre-trial brief which are -- concern quotations from the defendant in relation to Banja Luka. We simply say that there are there ample quotations from him, the gist of which -- and references to witnesses who have notes of them -- the gist of which is similar to the expressions of his opinion in the article, and it is inconceivable in a pre-trial brief of 152 pages that if evidence is said to be essential or central that it wasn't mentioned at all. Mr. Randal, it's true, is 69 and is retired from the Washington Post. Sixty-nine may be an old age for a war correspondent, although it's a young age for a judge. And Mr. Randal has -- is writing a book on terrorism. There's a lot of -- he has a continuing interest in this matter. Finally, the problems that were identified by Ms. Korner turn out to be not -- either not problems at all or problems with which the courts grapple regularly. She said, oh, well, there's no definition of a journalist. There is, of course, a definition of a journalist. You will find it in Attachment 5, the explanation or the accompanying notes to Article 79 of the Geneva Convention I. At paragraph 3260 - this is in Attachment 5 to our brief - it says that journalists in the Geneva Convention should bear the ordinary etymological meaning, although it calls to mind correspondents and writers writing for a daily newspaper. The use of the word in the convention covers the circle of people working for the press and so forth. And so that's -- that's the answer to that point. She says that -- how is the Court to tell whether the gist of the evidence is available. This is quite a familiar issue that courts decide in relation to protected material in the United Kingdom every week. So the problems that she identified are not insoluble problems. They're problems of fact and degree. Very often the solution is to be found -- for all the questions that may be asked about the principle, the solution will be found as a matter of common sense on the facts before the Court. And indeed that would be, we submit with respect, the solution in this case when the evidence is looked at is -- is pellucidly simple. Mr. Randal can give no central evidence either for the Prosecution or the Defence. The article is admissible. Whether the -- and the Defence have not indicated pursuant to Rule 90 any issue that is crucial or important to the defendant that they wish to obtain from Mr. Randal other than a fishing expedition into what they describe as background, so that in effect the insignificance of the article for the Court's determination of this defendant's guilt or innocence is plain on an examination, and we would submit that whatever questions may be raised about the -- or hypothetical quibbles with the language that we've suggested in the rule, that the rule will serve in most, if not all, cases to decide whether evidence -- and to some extent, of course, it is the instinct of the Judge developed by --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robertson, I think you have said all that. It's not necessary to repeat it. We have heard that. Your response was supposed to refer to some of the issues raised by Ms. Korner, and I think that you have had the opportunity of doing that. I'll turn to my colleagues to see if they have any questions to ask you. Judge Gunawardana, any questions? No questions. No questions. Very well. Judge Meron.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: The situation before us now in light of the e-mail which was mentioned is perhaps less than crystal clear. I would be grateful to the Prosecutor, to Ms. Korner, if she would tell us this: Assume that it is confirmed that Mr. Brdjanin does no longer contest the accuracy of the quotations. Would you still need in these circumstances a subpoena?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was about to raise this with Your Honours. First, the point that I'm trying to make is although Mr. Ackerman has sent this extraordinary e-mail not to the Court but to the appellant saying he no longer wishes to contest it, that admission has to be made before the Trial Chamber. Then if the Trial Chamber admits the article, we certainly on behalf of the Prosecution don't require Mr. Randal to attend. Mr. Ackerman, however, in order, as I understand it, still to have this article admitted says that we must call -- says the Trial Chamber must order the journalist to appear so he can question him about the context. But at the moment, as I say, all of this is unclear. We do not wish to call Mr. Randal. We took the statement from Mr. Randal to confirm the accuracy of the quotes. If those are no longer disputed, that ends our interest in calling him, provided the article is admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The technical service will help us to have a break because I've been told that there is no more tape. I've been told that there is no more videotape, but we have the transcript nevertheless. I think that everyone has had the opportunity of expressing themselves. I would like to thank my colleagues for all the questions they have asked, and obviously I would like to thank all of you, the amici curiae, the appellants, and the Prosecutor. And you have enabled us to deliberate at the moment. Thank you very much. The hearing is adjourned.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.05 p.m.
